title: How Amputation Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss amputation: the Aron Ralston self-amputation in 2003 (depicted in 127 Hours), the history of amputation from ancient times through Ambroise Paré's ligature, the tourniquet, anesthesia, the American Civil War, and Joseph Lister's antiseptic surgery. They cover causes (disease such as peripheral artery disease and diabetes, traumatic injury, cancer), the surgical process (skin, muscle, nerves, blood vessels, bone sanding, residual limb), wrong-site surgery and the Sign Your Site and time-out protocols, recovery and prosthetics, phantom limb pain and mirror box therapy, and body integrity identity disorder and acrotomophilia. A listener mail describes a testicular torsion case and prosthetic testicle.

segments.title: Opening banter and series context
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode as the follow-up to broken bones and replantation episodes, and mention upcoming topics of phantom limb pain and amputee sexual fetishes.

segments.title: Aron Ralston and 127 Hours
segments.summary: Discussion of Aron Ralston, trapped by a boulder in a canyon in 2003, who cut off his own arm below the elbow with a dull pocket knife, and of the film 127 Hours. The hosts note he hiked about six miles to get help.

segments.title: Why amputation is a last resort
segments.summary: Amputation is usually performed to stop an infection or dead tissue from spreading to the rest of the body, and is typically a last resort. Patients can still lead full lives afterward.

segments.title: Ancient amputation and early blood vessel ligature
segments.summary: Archaeological evidence of amputation about seven thousand years ago, when surgeons removed already-dead tissue because they could not control bleeding. Greeks and Romans began tying off blood vessels, but the technique was forgotten for centuries; wine and vinegar were used as antiseptics.

segments.title: Cauterization, Ambroise Paré, and the tourniquet
segments.summary: Surgeons later used cauterization with hot irons or boiling oil. Ambroise Paré, a French military surgeon, rediscovered ligature, aided by gunshot and cannonball injuries. The tourniquet was invented in 1674, and anesthetic gas arrived in the 1840s.

segments.title: American Civil War amputations and early surgical infection
segments.summary: The Civil War produced tens of thousands of amputations, giving rise to the term sawbones. Surgeons did not understand germs, and many patients died after amputation, with bacterial infection a major cause.

segments.title: Joseph Lister and antiseptic surgery
segments.summary: British surgeon Joseph Lister, known as the father of antiseptic surgery, used carbolic acid to spray tools, incisions, dressings and people, and promoted handwashing and clean gloves.

segments.title: Historical uses and causes of amputation
segments.summary: Amputation as religious sacrifice and as punishment in Rome and in the Code of Hammurabi. Modern causes include disease such as peripheral artery disease and diabetes (which the hosts say drives most US amputations), traumatic injury (leading cause under age fifty), and cancer.

segments.title: Preparing for amputation surgery
segments.summary: Pre-surgery meetings, anesthesia choices (usually general, not local), prosthetic measurement, and blood flow measurement to decide where to cut while preserving healthy tissue and joints. Emergency amputations skip planning.

segments.title: Steps of the amputation procedure
segments.summary: Walkthrough of the operation: cutting skin, muscle and nerves, ligating or cauterizing blood vessels, sawing and smoothing the bone, closing the residual limb, and draining with a tube when infection is a risk. Patients are monitored for weeks afterward.

segments.title: Phantom limb pain and mirror box therapy
segments.summary: Phantom limb pain occurs in most amputees and is chronic. The brain's map of the missing limb keeps sending signals. Treatments include mirror box therapy, imagined movement, and nerve stimulation. Earlier views held it was psychological; the hosts say it is now considered real.
